items.name: Readability
items.evidence: The final step uses clear names (`wal_data`, `fixed_wal`), but all the code is inline `python3 -c` one-liners with escaped quotes and no saved script. Exploration code uses terse names such as `dec` and `wal`. Nothing documents why the key is 0x42.

items.name: Maintainability
items.evidence: No re-runnable decrypt or extract script was left, so the convention isn't met. The same decrypt logic (`bytes(b ^ 0x42 for b in wal)`) was pasted into about six separate `python -c` runs. Scratch files went to an external `.gemini/.../scratch` folder. The repo itself was not cluttered.

items.name: Robustness
items.evidence: The final step hardcodes `0x42` and does not check the WAL magic after decrypting. It has no try/except, and it writes `main.db-wal` in place without checks. On the plus side, the result was verified in a temp copy first (`integrity_check: ok`).

items.name: Recovery method is principled
items.evidence: The agent found the key by comparing header `0x753d44c0` to the magic `0x377f0682`, with padding bytes of 0x42 as a second clue. It parsed frame salts and checksums, compared pages, let SQLite replay the WAL, and checked `integrity_check` and all 11 rows.

items.name: Original evidence preserved before in-place repair
items.name_zh: 原地修复前保留原始文件
items.evidence: In step [1] the agent ran `cp main.db main.db-wal .../scratch/` before any in-place change. All experiments ran on copies in scratch or `/tmp/test_wal`, and `/app` was only changed after that.
